parts: Lesson 21: Political Parties and Pressure Groups — Summary

In a representative democracy the people elect representatives, usually nominated by political parties. Parties are essential: they let people take part in elections, educate them and offer policy choices. Countries without parties, such as Libya, Oman, Qatar and the UAE, are not democracies.

A political party is an organised body of people who share common principles and goals and seek political power through constitutional means to put their policies into practice. Gilchrist: 'an organised group of citizens who profess the same political views and who, acting as a political unit, try to control the government'. Characteristics: an organised group; common principles and goals; aims at political power through collective effort; uses peaceful, constitutional methods — elections; converts its programme into government policy when in power.

Parties nominate candidates and campaign in elections; place their programmes before voters through manifestos; the majority party forms the government and implements policies; parties in minority form the opposition and keep a check on the government; they educate people and shape public opinion; articulate people's demands and convey them to the government; and link the people with government institutions. Indian parties have made representative government possible since independence.

The Indian National Congress (1885) began as an umbrella organisation; the Muslim League, Communist Party and Hindu Mahasabha also arose before independence. After 1947 the Congress dominated till 1967 (1952, 1957, 1962, 1967) — the 'one-party dominant system'. From 1967 the system changed; after 1977 the Janata Party government briefly suggested a two-party system. Since 1989 India has had coalition governments at the Centre; since 1999 two broad alliances — the BJP-led NDA and the Congress-led UPA. India now has a multi-party system.

Features today: many parties compete; a bi-nodal pattern around the Congress and BJP; regional parties play a vital role in forming Central governments and win favours for their States; elections are fought between coalitions; there are no permanent rulers or opposition; ideology has taken a back seat to a Common Minimum Programme and pragmatism; parties use emotive slogans ('Garibi Hatao', 'India Shining', 'Aam Aadmi') and chase short-term gains.

The Election Commission classifies parties as National, State and Registered (unrecognised), and allots election symbols to parties and candidates. A national party must be recognised in four or more States, or win a set share of Lok Sabha seats/votes (the textbook gives: at least 4% of Lok Sabha seats or 3.33% of assembly seats, and 6% of valid votes). In 2009 there were 7 national parties (Congress, BJP, CPI, CPI(M), BSP, NCP, RJD — the list changes; today, for example, the Aam Aadmi Party is national and the RJD is not), 34 State parties and 322 registered parties.

Policies: Congress (1885) — democracy, secularism, socialism; centrist; supports liberalisation (LPG) with welfare of weaker sections. BJP (1980, successor of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh) — nationalism and national integration, democracy, positive secularism, Gandhian socialism, value-based politics. Communist parties — CPI (1925) and CPI(M) (1964), based on Marxism-Leninism; for workers and peasants, socialism, land reforms; against capitalism and globalisation; ruled West Bengal, Kerala and Tripura. BSP (1984, Kanshi Ram; led by Mayawati) — for Dalits and the deprived, inspired by Phule, Periyar and Ambedkar; 'Sarvajan Hitay, Sarvajan Sukhay'. NCP (1999, Sharad Pawar, P.A. Sangma, Tariq Anwar; base in Maharashtra). RJD (1997, Lalu Prasad Yadav; Bihar) — social justice for backward castes and minorities.

Regional parties arose to fulfil regional aspirations: Trinamool Congress (West Bengal), Asom Gana Parishad (Assam), AIADMK and DMK (Tamil Nadu), National Conference (J&K), Samajwadi Party (UP), Shiromani Akali Dal (Punjab), Shiv Sena (Maharashtra), Telugu Desam (Andhra Pradesh). They have federalised the party system and strengthened cooperative federalism.

Interest groups are organised groups seeking to promote specific interests of their members; when they put pressure on the government to get their demands met, they become pressure groups. So all pressure groups are interest groups, but not all interest groups are pressure groups. Interest groups are formally organised, interest-oriented, softer and may or may not influence policy; pressure groups are strictly structured, pressure-focused, harsher and must influence policy.

Pressure groups differ from parties: they are not primarily political (e.g. the RSS is a cultural organisation), do not seek power directly, do not contest elections, need not have an ideology, and have specific interests, whereas parties seek power, contest elections, have ideologies and national programmes. Some are linked to parties (NSUI–Congress, ABVP–BJP; trade unions). Methods: appeals, petitions, demonstrations, picketing, lobbying, processions, media campaigns, satyagraha, strikes and boycotts. Examples in India: religious and caste groups, FICCI, AITUC, Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh, Kisan Sabha, government employees' unions, All Assam Students' Union.

CSOs are bodies formed by citizens on issues of common concern — environment, price rise, corruption, gender, child labour — and are a new form of mass pressure. Examples: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (Aruna Roy; led the movement for the Right to Information law), SEWA (Ela Bhatt; rights of women workers), Narmada Bachao Andolan (Medha Patkar), India Against Corruption (Anna Hazare), PUCL, NAPM, NAWO and the Meira Paibis of Manipur (supporting Irom Sharmila's long fast against AFSPA). They channel grievances, point out unfulfilled promises and train good, vigilant citizens.
